prompt: Every employee who completed the safety course received a certificate. Marcus did not receive a certificate. Which conclusion follows?
options: The safety course is harder than most employees had expected.
Everyone who received a certificate had completed the safety course.
Marcus did not complete the safety course.
Marcus was never told about the safety course by his supervisor.
Marcus is planning to take the safety course later this year.
explanation: This is the contrapositive: if completing the course guarantees a certificate, then no certificate means the course was not completed. The other options add facts the statements never supply. The claim that a certificate proves completion reverses the conditional the statements give, which is a different claim and not one they support.

prompt: A cafe owner says: "We introduced free wireless internet last month, and sales rose 20 percent, so the internet caused the increase." Which finding would most weaken this?
options: Sales at nearby cafes that offer no wireless internet fell slightly over the same month.
Some customers said they liked having the internet available.
The wireless internet cost considerably less to install than the owner had expected it to.
The cafe also began opening two hours earlier on the same day the internet was installed.
A few regular customers do not own laptops or tablets.
explanation: A second change made at the same time offers a rival explanation for the same rise, which is what undercuts a causal claim. The other options are about cost or opinion and leave the causal link untouched. A fall at cafes without internet points the other way and supports the owner rather than weakening him.

prompt: Argument: "The library should extend its opening hours, because a survey found that most students want to study later in the evening." What does this argument assume?
options: Students would actually use the library during the extended hours.
The library has never extended its hours at any point in the past.
No other study space in the town stays open later than the library does.
Studying later in the evening improves students' academic results.
Every student who answered the survey studies in the library regularly.
explanation: Wanting to study later is not the same as turning up, and the recommendation only works if stated preference becomes actual attendance. The other options are either irrelevant history or far stronger claims than the argument needs. The argument also does not need late study to improve results, since it rests on demand alone.

prompt: Argument: "Switching to the new supplier reduced our defect rate, since defects fell by a third after the switch." Which fact would most strengthen this?
options: The factory's defect rate had already been falling steadily for two years before the switch was made.
The new supplier is located considerably closer to the factory.
The new supplier charges slightly more per unit than the old one.
The old supplier had served the company for more than a decade.
No change was made to the production process during the same period.
explanation: Ruling out other changes in the same window is what turns a coincidence into evidence of cause. Location, tenure, and price say nothing about whether the supplier explains the fall in defects. A defect rate that was already falling before the switch would undercut the claim rather than support it, which is the reverse of what the question asks for.

prompt: All the paintings in the north gallery were produced after 1900. The museum's oldest painting hangs in the south gallery. Which statement must be true?
options: The museum's oldest painting was produced before 1900.
Every painting in the south gallery predates every painting in the north.
The museum's oldest painting is not in the north gallery.
No painting produced before 1900 hangs anywhere in the museum.
The south gallery holds more paintings than the north gallery does.
explanation: The second sentence states directly where the oldest painting hangs, so it is not in the north gallery. It does NOT follow that it predates 1900: the oldest painting could still be from 1950 if the whole collection is modern. It also does not follow that the museum holds nothing from before 1900, because the contents of the south gallery are never described.

prompt:
Passage: "Urban planners have long debated whether adding road capacity relieves congestion. The phenomenon known as induced demand suggests it often does not. When a route becomes faster, journeys that were previously not worth making become worthwhile: a shopper who had ordered a delivery drives to the store instead, a commuter who had settled for a nearby employer accepts a better job further away, and drivers who had shifted to other routes or to earlier departure times come back to the widened road. Each of those is a trip the old road never carried. Within a few years traffic on the widened route frequently returns to something close to its former level, and the time savings that justified the work disappear.

The evidence most often cited comes from comparisons across metropolitan areas, where the total distance driven has risen almost in proportion to the lane miles built. Critics of that evidence point out that capacity is not added at random. Lanes go where growth is already expected, so some of the extra driving would have appeared with or without the construction. Researchers have tried to separate the two effects by studying capacity that was planned decades earlier, for reasons unconnected to present-day growth, and they continue to find a large response.

Some planners conclude from all this that road widening is futile, since the queue it was built to remove reassembles itself. Others accept every step of the account and draw the opposite lesson. The extra journeys, they argue, represent real economic activity that congestion had been suppressing, and the appropriate measure of success is the number of trips served rather than the speed at which any one of them is made. On that reading a road that fills up again has not failed. It has been used." According to the passage, what does induced demand describe?
options: Congestion returning to its earlier level a few years after a road is widened.
A permanent reduction in the total number of car journeys made.
Drivers choosing public transport when roads become congested.
New journeys appearing once a route becomes faster.
The tendency of construction costs to rise during a road project.
explanation: The passage defines it as journeys that were not worth making becoming worthwhile once the route speeds up, together with the return of drivers who had diverted. The other options describe effects the passage never attributes to induced demand. The return of traffic to its former level is the consequence the passage draws from induced demand, not the definition of the term itself.

prompt:
Passage: "Few findings in transport research are as well established as induced demand, and few are as contested in what they are taken to prove. The finding itself is simple. When a congested road is widened, the new capacity is absorbed by journeys the old road did not carry. Some of those journeys belong to drivers who had been leaving early or taking a longer route to avoid the queue. Others are wholly new, made by people who had judged the trip not worth the time it used to take. Studies across many cities report that traffic volumes on widened roads return to near their former levels within about five years, and researchers on every side of the argument accept that pattern.

Where they part company is in what the pattern means. One group treats the return of congestion as evidence that widening fails on its own terms. The road was built to make journeys faster, speeds after five years are no better than before, and the promise on which the project was sold has not been kept. Members of this group tend to favor pricing the road at peak times, or moving the same passengers by rail or bus, on the ground that only a measure which changes behavior can hold a speed gain in place.

The second group accepts that description line by line and rejects the conclusion. A road carrying more vehicles at the same speed is carrying more people to more destinations. The journeys that appear are not phantom traffic but errands, deliveries and commutes that congestion had been holding back, and a policy that keeps the road empty by keeping those trips unmade has bought its speed at their expense. Judged by trips served rather than by travel speed, they argue, the widened road is doing more work than it was." How do the two groups of planners in the passage differ?
options: They disagree about whether drivers respond to changes in journey times.
They disagree about whether traffic returns to its former level after a road is widened.
They disagree about whether induced demand exists at all in modern cities.
They disagree about how expensive road widening projects usually are.
They disagree about which measure should count as success.
explanation: Both groups accept that traffic returns; they part company over whether to judge a road by travel speed or by total trips served. Neither disputes the existence of induced demand or the responsiveness of drivers, and cost is never mentioned. The option that has them disputing the return of traffic contradicts the one finding the passage says every side accepts.

prompt: Argument: "Our new training program works, because employees who took it were promoted more often than those who did not." Which finding would most weaken this?
options: The training program was delivered online rather than in person at the company offices.
A few employees found parts of the training repetitive.
The promotion rate across the whole company rose during the same period.
The program lasted three days rather than the planned five.
Managers selected their strongest performers to attend the training.
explanation: If the strongest performers were chosen to attend, they would likely have been promoted anyway, so the promotion gap reflects who was selected rather than what the training did. Format, length, and opinion do not disturb the causal claim. A company-wide rise in promotions is tempting but does not account for the gap between the two groups, which is what the argument rests on.

prompt: Argument: "The city should install more streetlights, since brighter streets will reduce nighttime accidents." Which assumption is required?
options: Nighttime accidents outnumber daytime accidents in the city.
Poor visibility contributes to at least some nighttime accidents.
Residents living near the streets have asked for better lighting.
Every nighttime accident in the city happens because a driver cannot see clearly.
Streetlights are the cheapest available road safety measure.
explanation: The argument only works if darkness is part of the problem; if visibility played no role, more light would change nothing. Cost, popularity, and the daytime comparison are not needed for the conclusion to follow. The claim that poor visibility explains every nighttime accident is far stronger than the argument requires.

prompt: Whenever the bakery runs a discount, it sells out before noon. Today the bakery did not sell out before noon. Which conclusion follows?
options: The bakery sells out before noon only if it runs a discount.
Customers were less interested in the bakery's products today.
The bakery will run a discount tomorrow to clear its stock.
The bakery baked more items today than it usually does.
The bakery did not run a discount today.
explanation: Again the contrapositive: a discount guarantees selling out, so not selling out means there was no discount. The remaining options speculate about causes and future behavior that the statements do not license. Nor does it follow that a discount is the only thing that can make the bakery sell out, since the premise runs in one direction only.

prompt: Argument: "Because employees at the branch that adopted flexible hours reported higher satisfaction, the company should adopt flexible hours everywhere to raise satisfaction overall." Which assumption does the argument depend on?
options: Satisfaction is the single most important measure of a company's health.
Employees at the company's other branches have already asked to be allowed to set their own working hours.
Every single employee at the branch preferred the flexible arrangement to the old fixed one.
The branch that adopted flexible hours is not unusual in ways that explain its higher satisfaction.
Flexible hours are administratively simpler to manage than fixed hours.
explanation: Generalizing from one branch requires that the branch be representative; if it differed in some relevant way, the result may not transfer. The unanimity and single-measure options are far stronger than the argument needs, and administrative simplicity is beside the point. A request already made at the other branches would be welcome news, but the inference does not need it.

prompt: A city claims its new recycling campaign worked because the tonnage sent to landfill fell last year. Which question would be most useful in evaluating that claim?
options: How much did the city spend designing the recycling campaign?
Did the total amount of waste generated in the city also fall last year?
Which neighborhoods received the campaign materials first?
Do most residents say they support recycling in principle?
How many residents recall having seen the recycling campaign's advertisements last year?
explanation: If total waste fell, landfill tonnage would drop whether or not anyone recycled more, so this question separates the two explanations. Spending, rollout order, and recall do not distinguish them. Support in principle is an attitude, and it would not show whether behavior or the volume of waste actually changed.

prompt:
Passage: "For much of the twentieth century, economists treated the firm as a rational actor that minimizes costs. Behavioral research has complicated that picture. Studies of managerial decision-making find that executives often persist with failing projects, committing further resources in order to justify what has already been spent. This pattern, sometimes called escalation of commitment, is hard to reconcile with pure cost minimization, because money already spent cannot be recovered and should therefore carry no weight in a decision about what to do next.

The evidence is not confined to the laboratory. Analyses of capital budgeting inside large firms find that a project with an unfavorable interim review is approved for further funding more often when the reviewing manager is the same person who approved the original proposal. Auditors of failed technology programs describe an identical sequence: a deadline slips, more staff are assigned, the revised deadline slips again, and the program is then defended in terms of the sum it has already consumed.

Defenders of the traditional model respond that persistence may be rational in a different sense. Canceling a project publicly is a dated admission that an earlier judgment was wrong, and a manager whose next position depends on a record of completed work has reason to postpone that admission. On this reading the manager is optimizing after all, but the thing being optimized is a career rather than the firm's balance sheet. The behavior looks irrational only if the analyst assumes that the decision maker and the firm want the same thing.

The reply is not a full defense of the original model, since it concedes that the firm's costs are not what the manager is minimizing. What it does suggest is that the choice on offer is between two accounts of whose interests a decision serves, rather than between reason and error." What is the primary purpose of the passage?
options: To trace how the view economists take of the firm changed across the twentieth century.
To present a challenge to a traditional model and a response to that challenge.
To recommend specific practices that managers should adopt when projects fail.
To argue that the traditional economic model of the firm should be abandoned entirely.
To describe a series of experiments conducted on executives at large firms.
explanation: The passage lays out the traditional view, presents behavioral evidence against it, and then gives the traditional side's reply. It stops short of endorsing either position or recommending anything. Nor is the passage a chronology of the discipline: it sets out one challenge and one reply rather than a sequence of changing views.

prompt:
Passage: "Escalation of commitment is the tendency to put further resources into a course of action that is already failing. Laboratory work has documented it for decades. Participants who personally chose an initial investment allocate more to it after learning that it is losing money than participants who inherited the same investment from somebody else. The effect survives when the stakes are raised, and it survives when participants are warned about it in advance.

Economists who model the firm as a cost minimizer have found the pattern awkward. Money already spent cannot be recovered, so a decision about the next unit of spending should depend only on what that unit will earn. A manager who reasons instead from the sum already committed is, on the standard account, simply making an error, and the error should be trained away.

Defenders of the standard account have offered a reply that keeps the rationality assumption and moves the objective. A manager does not face the problem the firm faces. Canceling a project is a public and dated admission that an earlier judgment was wrong, and it is the manager, not the firm, who carries that admission into the next promotion review. Continuing the project keeps the verdict open for another year. Seen this way the manager is choosing well, given what the manager is trying to protect, and the apparent error is an artifact of assuming that the manager's objective and the firm's objective are one and the same.

Critics of the reply note that it explains the behavior without excusing it. If the incentive is the cause, a firm that understands the cause can remove it, by having interim reviews conducted by managers who had no part in approving the original proposal, and by treating an early cancellation as a decision worth crediting rather than a failure worth recording." The defenders' response suggests that escalation of commitment is:
options: less common among executives than the behavioral research claims.
rational for the firm as a whole once the full cost of abandoning a project is counted.
rational once the manager's own interests are the thing being optimized.
a phenomenon that appears only in firms already facing serious financial difficulty.
irrational from any point of view that could reasonably be adopted.
explanation: Their reply relocates the objective rather than denying the behavior: it is rational, but with respect to the manager's career rather than the firm's costs. They do not dispute how often it occurs or restrict it to struggling firms. The reply moves the objective to the manager, so reading the persistence as rational for the firm keeps the wrong party in view.

prompt: Argument: "Cities with more parks report higher resident wellbeing, so building parks raises wellbeing." Which finding would most weaken this argument?
options: Wealthier cities tend both to build more parks and to score higher on wellbeing for unrelated reasons.
Some residents visit their local parks only a handful of times each year.
The study counted the number of parks in each city rather than measuring the total area of parkland available to residents.
Wellbeing surveys are conducted at different times of year in different cities in the study.
Park maintenance budgets vary considerably between the cities studied.
explanation: A common cause behind both variables explains the correlation without any causal arrow from parks to wellbeing, which is the strongest form of attack here. Infrequent visits, budget variation, and survey timing weaken the evidence only marginally. Counting parks rather than measuring parkland area is a quibble about the measure that leaves the causal claim standing.

prompt: Argument: "No member of the research team has published on marine biology, so the team is unqualified to review the marine survey." Which best describes the flaw?
options: It relies on a survey whose sample was far too small to support any general conclusion.
It draws a conclusion about a group from evidence about one member of it.
It confuses the order in which two related events actually occurred.
It treats publication in a field as the only possible source of competence in it.
It uses a key term in one sense in the premise and in a different sense in the conclusion.
explanation: The argument equates "has not published" with "is unqualified", ignoring that expertise can come from practice, training, or related fields. No sample or ordering is involved, and the evidence concerns every member rather than one. No term shifts its meaning between the premise and the conclusion either.

prompt: Argument: "The redesigned checkout page caused the rise in completed purchases, since completions rose 18 percent in the month after launch." Which fact would most strengthen this?
options: Visitors randomly shown the old page in the same month completed far fewer purchases.
The redesign was praised by several user experience specialists.
Completed purchases in the month before the redesign launched were at their usual seasonal level.
The company's total advertising spend was unchanged throughout that same month.
The redesigned page loads marginally faster than the previous version.
explanation: A randomized comparison run in the same period removes essentially every rival explanation at once, which is stronger than merely holding one other factor constant. Praise and load time say nothing about causation, and constant advertising rules out only a single alternative. A normal seasonal baseline in the prior month, like unchanged advertising, closes one alternative explanation rather than all of them at once.

prompt: A factory's records show that whenever the night shift is understaffed, output falls below target. Last Tuesday output met its target. Which statement must be true about last Tuesday?
options: The night shift was not understaffed.
The factory hired additional workers for the night shift.
The night shift is understaffed on most of the days when output falls below target.
Output exceeded the target by a substantial margin.
The night shift produced more units than the day shift did that day.
explanation: Understaffing guarantees missing the target, so meeting it rules out understaffing. Nothing follows about relative shift output, hiring, or the size of the margin. It also does not follow that understaffing accounts for most of the days when output falls short, since the records run the other way.

prompt: Argument: "Since the region's farms produce more food than its population consumes, no one in the region should go hungry." Which assumption is required?
options: The region's farms will maintain their current output in future years.
Everyone in the region can afford to buy as much food as they need.
The region imports no food at all from neighboring areas.
Every farm in the region grows the same variety of crops.
The food produced is actually distributed to those who need it.
explanation: Aggregate sufficiency says nothing about who gets what; the conclusion needs distribution to reach the people who need food. Future output, imports, and crop variety are not required for the inference as stated. Universal ability to pay is stronger than the argument needs, because food could reach people without being bought.

prompt:
Passage: "Antibiotic resistance is often described as a crisis of the near future, but the mechanism behind it is old. Bacteria have carried and traded resistance genes for as long as antibiotics have existed in nature, which is far longer than they have existed in medicine. Soil frozen before the first clinical use of penicillin holds organisms with resistance genes, and so do bacteria recovered from caves and sediments that no manufactured drug has ever reached.

What has changed is the intensity of selection. A resistance gene is not free. It usually costs the cell something to carry, which is why resistant strains do not simply take over in the absence of a drug. Introduce the drug and the accounting reverses. Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria efficiently, so the survivors inherit a population with their competition removed, and a gene that was rare becomes common within a few bacterial generations. Widespread clinical prescribing and routine agricultural use apply that pressure to enormous populations, continuously, in hospitals, in livestock, and in the water that leaves both.

Reducing total antibiotic use is therefore the primary lever available. It is also politically difficult. The benefit of restraint is diffuse and delayed. It is spread across every future patient and can never be credited to any particular decision not to prescribe. The cost falls immediately and visibly on the individual patient who is told that a prescription would do no good, or on the farmer asked to raise animals without a routine additive in the feed. Programs that succeed tend to be the ones that move the decision away from that encounter, by setting prescribing rules for a whole hospital or by regulating agricultural use directly, rather than by appealing to restraint one consultation at a time." According to the passage, what has changed in recent times?
options: The willingness of farmers to reduce their use of antibiotics.
Bacteria have only recently developed the ability to exchange genes.
The intensity of selection favoring resistant bacteria.
The efficiency with which antibiotics kill the bacteria that are susceptible to them.
The speed at which new antibiotics can be brought to market.
explanation: The passage says the mechanism is old and identifies intensity of selection as what has changed. It explicitly denies that gene exchange is new, and never discusses development speed or a change in willingness. Efficient killing of susceptible bacteria is how the selection works, not the thing the passage says has changed.

prompt:
Passage: "Antibiotic resistance is not a new biological phenomenon. Resistance genes predate medicine, and bacteria have always traded them across species lines. What medicine changed is how strongly those genes are favored. A drug that kills susceptible cells efficiently hands the survivors an empty field, and widespread clinical and agricultural use applies that pressure to very large populations without pause.

Several responses are available in principle. New drugs can be developed, though the commercial case for them is weak, since a genuinely novel antibiotic would be held in reserve and sold sparingly. Diagnostics can be improved, so that a physician learns within minutes whether an infection is bacterial at all rather than prescribing against the possibility that it is. Infection control can be tightened, so that resistant strains move less readily from one patient to the next. Each of these helps. None of them removes the pressure that creates resistance in the first place.

That leaves reducing total antibiotic use as the primary lever, and surveys find remarkably little disagreement about it. Physicians describe resistance as a serious threat and report prescribing more than they believe is necessary. Farmers and veterinarians report the same discomfort about routine additives in animal feed. The obstacle, then, is not doubt about the science, and it is not a shortage of other measures to try alongside restraint. It is that restraint pays out to the wrong person at the wrong time: the benefit is diffuse and delayed, spread thinly across patients who will fall ill years from now, while the cost falls at once and in full on the patient sent home without a prescription and on the farmer asked to go without." The final sentence suggests that the main obstacle to reducing antibiotic use is:
options: the difficulty of measuring how much antibiotic is used in agriculture.
a lack of scientific agreement about how resistance actually spreads.
the reluctance of patients and farmers to accept that resistance is a real problem.
the absence of any effective alternative treatment for common infections.
an asymmetry between who bears the cost and who receives the benefit.
explanation: The passage contrasts a diffuse, delayed benefit with an immediate, concentrated cost, which is precisely a cost-benefit asymmetry. It reports no scientific disagreement, and neither alternatives nor measurement are mentioned. Disbelief is ruled out directly, since the passage reports that the people asked to show restraint already describe resistance as serious.

prompt: Argument: "Our premium subscribers report far higher satisfaction than free users, so upgrading users to premium would raise satisfaction across the base." Which finding would most weaken this?
options: The satisfaction survey was sent to premium subscribers slightly more often.
Premium subscribers use the service for more hours each week than free users do.
Users who were already most satisfied are the ones who chose to upgrade.
Premium subscribers pay a fee that free users have chosen not to pay.
Some premium features are also available to free users on a trial basis.
explanation: Self-selection reverses the causal direction: satisfaction produced the upgrade rather than the upgrade producing satisfaction, so moving people up would not carry the effect with it. The fee is already implied, survey frequency is a minor bias, and trials would if anything narrow the gap. Heavier use by premium subscribers sits comfortably with the upgrade working and so does not undercut the recommendation.

prompt: Argument: "A tax on sugary drinks will reduce obesity, because consumption of those drinks falls sharply when their price rises." Which assumption is required?
options: Consumers do not replace the forgone drinks with other equally caloric products.
The revenue raised by the tax will be spent on public health programs.
The tax will apply to every sugary drink sold in the country without exception.
Sugary drinks are by a clear margin the single largest source of calories in the average diet.
Producers will pass the entire cost of the tax on to consumers immediately.
explanation: If people substitute other high-calorie items, consumption of the taxed drinks falls without obesity changing, breaking the chain from price to outcome. The argument does not need sugary drinks to be the largest source, nor any particular use of the revenue. The tax also need not reach every drink without exception for the conclusion to follow.

prompt: A hospital introduced a checklist that measurably reduced surgical errors, yet its reported complication rate rose in the following year. Which of the following, if true, best explains this?
options: The hospital performed slightly fewer operations than it had the previous year.
Several surgeons at the hospital said that the checklist made them more careful during the operations themselves.
The checklist added several minutes to the preparation time before each and every operation.
The checklist also introduced systematic reporting of complications that had previously gone unrecorded.
Surgeons at the hospital were initially skeptical about adopting the checklist.
explanation: If more complications are now being recorded, the reported rate can rise while the true rate falls; the paradox dissolves once measurement changes. Preparation time, skepticism, and volume do not reconcile fewer errors with more reported complications. Greater care reported by surgeons explains the fall in errors and leaves the rise in reported complications exactly as puzzling as before.

prompt: Argument: "Either we cut the research budget or we will not survive the downturn. We must therefore cut the research budget." Which best describes the reasoning flaw?
options: It uses a key term in one sense in the premise and in another sense in the conclusion.
It assumes the two stated options are the only ones available.
It mistakes a necessary condition for a sufficient one.
It generalizes from a sample that is unlikely to be representative.
It appeals to the authority of people who are not experts on the question.
explanation: The argument presents a false dilemma: other responses to a downturn exist, and the conclusion only follows if the two alternatives really are exhaustive. No authority is cited and no sample is involved. No term shifts its meaning between the premise and the conclusion, so a definitional complaint misses what has gone wrong here.

prompt: Every applicant who was interviewed had passed the written test. Some applicants who passed the written test were not offered a position. Which statement must be true?
options: Some applicants who were interviewed were not offered a position.
Some applicants were not offered a position.
Every applicant who passed the written test was interviewed at some stage.
No applicant was offered a position without first being interviewed.
Some applicants who passed the written test were interviewed.
explanation: The second premise states outright that some applicants passed the written test and were not offered a position, so it follows with certainty that some applicants were not offered a position. Nothing else here is guaranteed. The first premise makes interviewees a subset of test-passers, not the reverse, so it does not establish that every passer was interviewed, and it does not establish that a position required an interview. The claim that some interviewees were rejected does not follow either, because the rejected passers could all be people who were never interviewed. It is not even guaranteed that anyone was interviewed at all, so the claim that some test-passers reached an interview does not follow either.

prompt: Argument: "The decline in the songbird population is caused by pesticide use, since the decline began in the same decade that pesticide application became widespread." Which fact would most strengthen this?
options: Pesticide use in the region rose again in the decade after the songbird decline had already begun.
Pesticide manufacturers expanded their production capacity considerably during that same decade.
Songbird numbers held steady in an otherwise similar region where pesticides were never adopted.
Several other bird species also declined somewhat over the same period.
Farmers in the region reported higher crop yields after adopting pesticides.
explanation: A comparable region without the suspected cause and without the effect is the closest thing to a control, which is what turns coincident timing into evidence. Production capacity and yields concern pesticides but not birds, and other species declining is consistent with many causes. A later rise in pesticide use, after the decline was under way, works against the timing the argument depends on.

prompt:
Passage: "The standard account of the industrial revolution credits technological invention. A sequence of machines appeared, and industry followed. Recent economic history has emphasized something less visible, namely the price of the things a machine replaces. In regions where wages were high relative to the price of fuel, a machine that burned coal in order to save labor paid for itself quickly. Where labor was cheap and fuel was dear, the same machine was a poor investment, and it was not bought.

The evidence assembled for this view is comparative. Wage series and fuel prices reconstructed for several eighteenth-century economies show a wide spread, with some regions paying skilled workers several times what their counterparts earned elsewhere while sitting on coalfields that made fuel unusually cheap. Early spinning and pumping machinery, on this reading, was installed first in exactly those places, and installed elsewhere only later, as improvements in design cut the fuel each machine consumed and made it profitable at lower wages. The invention was available in both settings. The reason to use it was not.

On this account the machines were not so much the cause of industrial change as the response to it, and the question worth asking shifts from why the inventions were made to why they were worth installing.

Critics of the wage explanation raise two objections. The first is empirical. There are documented cases of adoption running ahead of any wage advantage that can be shown, which the account ought not to permit. The second objection is that the explanation understates why the inventions existed to be adopted at all. Scientific societies, instrument makers and a culture of published experiment made a whole class of machines thinkable, and no arrangement of prices will produce a machine that nobody has yet designed." Which of the following best expresses the wage explanation described in the passage?
options: High wages relative to fuel costs made mechanization commercially worthwhile.
Machines were invented in regions where scientific institutions were strongest.
Mechanization spread fastest in the regions where fuel was expensive relative to wages.
Workers in high-wage regions actively resisted the introduction of machinery.
Technological invention was the primary driver of industrial change.
explanation: The passage states that where wages were high relative to fuel prices, replacing labor with machines paid for itself, which is the wage explanation in a sentence. The institutions option belongs to the critics, and the invention-first option is the standard account the passage is contrasting with. The option that reverses the ratio, setting expensive fuel against cheap labor, inverts the condition the passage actually states.

prompt:
Passage: "Why did mechanized industry take hold where and when it did? The standard answer points to invention. A newer answer points to prices. Machines substitute fuel and capital for human labor, so a machine is worth installing where labor is dear and fuel is cheap, and not worth installing where the ratio runs the other way. Historians working in this tradition have reconstructed wage and fuel series for a number of eighteenth-century regions, and they argue that the earliest adopters were the places with the most expensive labor relative to coal.

The argument makes a testable prediction rather than merely redescribing what happened. If prices drove adoption, then ranking regions by the ratio of wages to fuel prices should broadly predict the order in which they mechanized, and a machine available everywhere should arrive last where labor was cheapest. Supporters point to spinning and to mine pumping as cases that behave in just that way, and to the later spread of the same machines into lower-wage regions once improvements in design cut the fuel each one consumed.

Opponents attack the prediction directly. They point to industries that mechanized in low-wage settings well before any wage advantage can be documented, which is the kind of case the account is not supposed to allow. They add that the explanation leaves the inventions themselves unaccounted for. A price signal tells a manufacturer that a machine would be profitable. It does not produce the machine, and the institutions that trained instrument makers and circulated experimental results have to carry that part of the story. Supporters reply that the two explanations answer different questions, one about invention and one about use, and are therefore not in competition at all." Which finding would most undermine the wage explanation?
options: A region with high wages that also happened to have unusually strong scientific institutions.
A high-wage region that adopted machinery only once its fuel prices had fallen.

The trouble is that many tardigrade species produce almost no trehalose at all. Researchers looking for what else might be responsible identified a family of proteins found in no other animal. Unlike ordinary proteins, these have no fixed shape while the cell is wet. Whether this fully explains tardigrade resilience remains unsettled. Trehalose accumulates in the membranes and takes the place of the water that is leaving the cell.
Reactive molecules are expelled from the cell before they can reach and damage the animal's DNA.
The animal's unusual proteins are broken down and their components are recycled into new membranes.
The internal temperature falls until it approaches absolute zero and metabolism stops.
explanation: The passage states that the unusual proteins vitrify as water leaves, so the cytoplasm becomes a glass rather than a liquid and the suspended molecules are immobilized. arguing that the container mattered because of the standards agreed for it rather than the box itself.
describing how the decline of the old finger piers reshaped the economies of port cities everywhere.
comparing the cost of moving goods by ocean with the cost of moving the same goods by rail.

The reluctance of respondents to record activities that carry some social judgment.
The expense of running direct observational studies alongside the diaries themselves.
The difficulty of converting the entries in a diary into a monetary value.

Passage: "Negligence law asks whether a defendant behaved as a reasonable person would have behaved in the circumstances. The objectivity is not absolute. A child is judged against other children of similar age and experience, and a defendant with a physical disability is judged against a reasonable person with that disability. A doctor is held to the standard of a competent doctor, not of a competent layperson. Defenders answer that the line is not arbitrary even if it is not derived. The characteristics that earn an adjustment are those the defendant could not have altered and could not reasonably have been expected to compensate for, while the characteristics that earn none, such as inexperience, carelessness or a hot temper, are precisely those the law wishes to give people a reason to work on. On this reading the standard is not a description of ordinary behavior at all. It is an instruction about the conduct the community will insist on, and the apparent inconsistency is the shape of a policy rather than the flaw of a definition." The reference to a doctor in the second paragraph serves primarily to:

show that different courts have applied the reasonable person standard inconsistently to similar facts.
suggest that defendants with expert training are treated more leniently than ordinary defendants are.
give a further instance of the standard being adjusted to a characteristic of the defendant.
illustrate how hard juries find it to reconstruct what was in a defendant's mind at the time.
explanation: The doctor sits in a short list with the child and the defendant with a physical disability, all offered as cases where the supposedly objective standard bends to something about the person being judged, which sets up the criticism that follows. prompt:
Passage: "Software licenses that permit copying come in two broad families. Permissive licenses let anyone use the code for any purpose, including inside a product whose own source is never released. Reciprocal licenses, often called copyleft, attach a condition: anyone who distributes a modified version must release the modifications under the same terms. Both families rely on copyright rather than opposing it. A copyleft license is enforceable only because the author holds the exclusive right to control copying and has chosen to license that right conditionally.

The practical difference shows up in how companies behave. A firm that builds a product on permissive code may keep its own changes private, and many firms do, so improvements made inside the firm never return to the project. A firm that builds on copyleft code must publish its modifications if it ships the result, so the project receives the improvements, but some firms decline to build on that code at all. Neither outcome is obviously better for a project, and the two families have persisted side by side for thirty years without either displacing the other.

A complication has grown with the shift to software delivered over a network. Copyleft conditions are typically triggered by distribution, and a company that runs modified code on its own servers and offers the result as a service distributes nothing to anyone. The modifications stay private and the reciprocity the license was written to secure does not operate. Newer licenses attempt to close this by treating network access as a triggering event, but they are less widely adopted, partly because the obligation they create is harder for a company's lawyers to bound: it can reach code that was never intended to be shipped to anyone." It can be inferred from the passage that a company running modified copyleft software only on its own servers is:
options: in violation of its license for as long as it declines to publish the modifications it has made.
obliged to obtain a second, permissive license from the author before it may run the code at all.
barred by the terms of the original license from making any modifications to the code.
prevented by copyright law from offering the modified software to the public as a service.
not required by a distribution-triggered license to release its modifications.
explanation: The passage says the condition is triggered by distribution, that such a company distributes nothing, and that the modifications therefore stay private, which is why newer licenses had to invent a network trigger. That is the opposite of a violation, and nothing in the passage requires a second license, forbids modification, or bars offering the result as a service.

Thirteen open-ocean experiments carried out between 1993 and 2009 confirmed the bloom in every case.

The proposal that follows is to use this response to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Phytoplankton take up carbon as they grow, and if enough of the resulting organic matter sinks below the depth at which water mixes back to the surface, that carbon is out of the atmosphere for centuries. The step that matters is therefore not the bloom but the sinking, and the sinking is exactly what the experiments measured least well. Most of the carbon fixed in a bloom is eaten by grazers or respired by bacteria within the upper hundred meters and returns to the surface within a year. Estimates of the fraction that reaches depth vary by more than a factor of ten between studies, and the studies with the most careful measurement generally report the lowest figures.

It is worth being precise about what this uncertainty licenses. It does not show that fertilization cannot sequester carbon, and the persistent claim that the experiments failed misrepresents them. What it shows is that the quantity a purchaser of carbon credits would be paying for has not been measured to anything approaching the accuracy such a market would require. Enthusiasm has run consistently ahead of the measurement, and the appropriate response is better measurement rather than either commercial deployment or dismissal." The author's attitude toward ocean iron fertilization is best described as:
options: unconvinced that the effect has been measured well enough to sell, yet unwilling to dismiss it.
confident that the method will prove to be an effective and cheap means of removing carbon.
persuaded by the thirteen experiments that the approach has been shown to be unworkable.
indifferent to the question, on the ground that the underlying chemistry is already settled.
critical of the scientists who designed and carried out the thirteen open-ocean experiments.
explanation: The closing paragraph refuses both endings: it says the uncertainty does not show that fertilization cannot work and that calling the experiments failures misrepresents them, while also saying the quantity a buyer would pay for is nowhere near well enough measured for a market. The arrangement creates a second problem in place of the first. Each outlet's profit depends on its own service and cleanliness, but the value of the brand depends on all of them together. An operator who lets standards slip captures the whole saving and bears only a small share of the damage, which is spread across every other outlet in the system. Courts have generally enforced them, reasoning that the restrictions protect the asset the franchisee bought access to.

Economists have noted a pattern that follows from this logic. Franchising is most common where customers are travelers rather than residents, since a customer who will never return has no way to punish a bad outlet except by avoiding the brand everywhere. It is least common where the service is complex enough that quality cannot be specified in a contract. Where a location is both heavily traveled and highly visible, the franchisor tends to own the outlet outright, keeping under direct control those outlets whose failure would do the most damage to the brand." Based on the passage, which business would be LEAST likely to be organized as a franchise?

A law practice whose attorneys handle unusual and complicated commercial disputes.
A chain of coffee shops operating inside the terminals of large regional airports.
A chain of quick-service restaurants located at rest stops on major highways.
A chain of car rental counters located in the concourses of busy railway stations.

prompt:
Passage: "When speakers of mutually unintelligible languages are thrown together and need to trade, they improvise a pidgin: a stripped vocabulary borrowed mostly from the dominant group, almost no inflection, and word order that varies from one speaker to the next. A pidgin is nobody's first language. What interests linguists is what happens in the next generation. Children raised in a pidgin-speaking community do not learn a pidgin. They produce a creole, which has consistent word order, a system of markers for tense and aspect, embedded clauses, and the other machinery that pidgins lack.

One influential account treats this as evidence for an innate language faculty. On this view the children are not learning the grammar, because the grammar is not present in what they hear. They are supplying it, and the striking resemblances among creoles that arose on different continents from unrelated source languages reflect the shape of the faculty itself rather than any shared history.

The competing account does not deny that children build the grammar, only that they build it out of nothing. It points out that the adults around them were not speaking a uniform pidgin. Each spoke a pidgin shaped by his own first language, so the input was variable rather than empty, and a learner facing variable input has good reason to settle on whichever pattern is most frequent and most reliably understood. Similar solutions on different continents would then reflect similar pressures rather than a shared innate template.

Deciding between the accounts has been difficult because the historical record is thin. The pidgin stage is rarely documented, and it is precisely the input to the first creole-speaking generation that would have to be reconstructed. Studies of newly formed sign languages have been offered as a living substitute, though whether a deaf community's situation is comparable remains contested." The passage suggests that the two accounts disagree principally about:
options: whether a creole ends up with more grammatical structure than the pidgin that preceded it.
whether the children of a pidgin-speaking community acquire the pidgin as a first language.
the character of the linguistic input available to the first generation of creole speakers.
whether creoles that arose on different continents in fact resemble one another closely.
whether the newly formed sign languages now under study should be classified as creoles.
explanation: The second account is described as agreeing that children build the grammar and disputing only that they build it out of nothing, on the ground that the adult input was variable rather than empty. Both accounts accept that creoles are more structured than pidgins, that children do not acquire a pidgin as a first language, and that distant creoles resemble one another; the sign language question is raised as a possible way to settle the disagreement, not as its subject.

prompt:
Passage: "A patent claim is a sentence that marks a boundary. Anything inside it infringes, and anything outside it does not. The virtue of insisting on the literal words is notice: a competitor can read the claim and design around it with confidence. The vice is that an infringer who makes an insubstantial change escapes, and that a claim drafted years before a technology matured may not reach a variation nobody had thought to describe.

Most patent systems answer with a doctrine of equivalents, under which a device outside the literal words may still infringe if it performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. The doctrine is old and uneasy. Every application of it enlarges a boundary the public was invited to rely on, and the enlargement is discovered only after a court has ruled.

Courts have accordingly hedged the doctrine with limits. The most consequential is prosecution history estoppel. If, during examination, an applicant narrowed a claim in order to win allowance over the prior art, he may not later recapture the surrendered territory by calling the surrendered variation an equivalent. The rule is severe, and it is meant to be. The applicant chose the words, the public read the file, and the narrowing was the price of the grant.

The result is a system that is neither purely literal nor purely purposive, and commentators disagree about whether the balance is stable. Some argue that the estoppel rule has made the doctrine so hard to invoke that it no longer performs the function it was created to perform. Others reply that its value lies less in the cases it wins than in the cases it deters, which by their nature cannot be counted." The statement that the applicant chose the words and the public read the file serves primarily to:
options: criticize applicants who draft their claims carelessly during the examination process.
explain why patent claims are so often drafted years before a technology has matured.
question whether a doctrine of equivalents ought to be recognized by courts at all.
justify the severity of a rule the passage has just described as severe.
identify the disagreement among commentators about whether the present balance is stable.
explanation: The sentence comes immediately after the passage calls prosecution history estoppel severe and says the severity is intended, and it supplies the reasons for that intention: the applicant wrote the narrowing and the public relied on it. It is not an attack on careless drafting, not an argument against the doctrine of equivalents, and not the commentators' disagreement, which arrives in the following paragraph.

prompt:
Passage: "Measuring the distance to a remote galaxy requires an object whose true brightness is known, since apparent brightness then gives distance directly. A particular class of exploding star has served this purpose for three decades. These explosions occur when a dense stellar remnant draws matter from a companion until it passes a threshold mass and detonates, and because that threshold is set by physics rather than by circumstance, the explosions were expected to be nearly identical.

They are not identical, but they are correctable. Brighter examples fade more slowly, and a single empirical relation between peak brightness and rate of fading reduces the scatter enough to make these objects the most precise distance indicators available at large separations. It was this correction, applied to distant explosions in the late 1990s, that produced the evidence that the expansion of the universe is accelerating.

The correction is where the difficulty now sits. The relation between brightness and fade rate is empirical, calibrated on nearby explosions whose distances are known by other means, and then applied to distant ones that occurred in younger galaxies of different chemical composition. If the relation drifts with the age or composition of the host galaxy, the calibration carries an error along with the measurement, and that error would be systematic rather than random, so no amount of additional data would average it away. Surveys have looked for such a drift and have set limits on it, but the limits are not tight enough to be ignored in the current generation of measurements, where the disagreement between different methods of measuring the expansion rate now exceeds the quoted uncertainty of either.

Nothing here suggests the acceleration is an artifact. It suggests that the next advance will come from understanding the explosions rather than from observing more of them." The passage indicates that a drift in the brightness-fade relation would be especially troubling because it would:
options: leave the explosions too faint to be observed at the largest separations now under study.
establish that the expansion of the universe is not in fact accelerating after all.
force astronomers to give up empirical calibration in favor of purely theoretical models.
remove the present disagreement between different methods of measuring the expansion rate.
introduce an error that collecting more observations would not reduce.
explanation: The passage says the error would be systematic rather than random, so no amount of additional data would average it away, which is exactly why a drift is worse than ordinary imprecision. The passage explicitly denies that any of this shows the acceleration to be an artifact, and it neither predicts an abandonment of empirical calibration nor suggests that a drift would resolve the disagreement between methods.

prompt:
Passage: "Radio spectrum was for most of the twentieth century assigned by administrative hearing. An applicant argued that granting it a license would serve the public interest, and a regulator chose among the arguments. The procedure was slow, the criteria were vague, and the licenses that emerged were worth a great deal more than the applicants had paid for them, which is a description of a process that rewards advocacy rather than use.

Auctions replaced hearings in many countries during the 1990s, and the design problem turned out to be harder than it looked. Spectrum licenses are not independent goods. A carrier that wins a block covering one city and not the city next to it may have bought something close to worthless, so bidders need to express what they will pay for combinations rather than for single items. Selling each license separately by sealed bid forces every bidder to guess what the others will do and to risk winning half of what it needs, an exposure that makes cautious bidders bid low and aggressive ones overpay.

The response was the simultaneous ascending auction, in which every license stays open while bidding continues, so a bidder losing one piece of a plan can withdraw from the rest before the sale closes. It works, in the sense that it usually assigns licenses to the bidders that value them most and raises substantial revenue, but it introduced problems of its own. A long open auction lets bidders signal to one another through the trailing digits of their bids, and several regulators have had to write rules against the practice.

The literature that grew out of these sales is now cited well beyond spectrum. Its central lesson is that a market does not simply exist to be used. Its rules determine what it can express, and those rules have to be designed for the goods actually being sold." Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The rules of an auction, rather than the decision to hold one, determine how well spectrum is assigned.
Administrative hearings distributed radio spectrum more fairly than the auctions that replaced them.
The simultaneous ascending auction has eliminated the possibility of collusion among bidders.
Spectrum licenses ought to be sold one at a time rather than in combinations of several blocks.
Regulators in the 1990s badly underestimated the revenue that a spectrum sale could raise.
explanation: The passage moves from a bad assignment procedure to auctions, then spends most of its length on why the particular auction design mattered and how one design fixed an exposure problem while creating a signaling problem, closing with the statement that a market's rules determine what it can express. It never prefers hearings, never claims collusion was eliminated, and its argument about combinations runs against selling licenses one at a time.

prompt:
Passage: "For twenty years microcredit was described as a way out of poverty. Small loans, made mostly to women, without collateral and at interest rates far below those charged by local moneylenders, would fund small enterprises whose profits would raise household income. The claim rested largely on comparisons between borrowers and non-borrowers, which is a weak design: people who seek a loan differ from people who do not in ambition, in existing business activity and in access to information, and every one of those differences also predicts income.

A series of randomized evaluations conducted in six countries addressed that objection by randomizing which neighborhoods a lender entered. The results were consistent and modest. Borrowing rose, business investment rose somewhat, and household income and consumption were essentially unchanged. Measures of empowerment and of children's schooling moved very little. The pattern held across quite different settings, which is unusual enough to be worth noting on its own.

Two readings of the same result compete. The first is that microcredit does not do what was claimed for it, and that the enthusiasm reflected a narrative rather than evidence. The second is that the evaluations measured the wrong quantity. An average conceals a distribution, and a program that helps a minority substantially while leaving the majority unaffected produces exactly the average that was observed. Later analyses looking for such heterogeneity have found some, concentrated among households that already ran a business before the loan arrived.

What is no longer seriously disputed is the scale of the original claim. Microcredit is a useful financial instrument that lets a household manage timing, absorb a shock and avoid a moneylender, and that is not a small thing. It is not a mechanism for lifting large numbers of people out of poverty, and the evidence that it is has not appeared." The passage suggests that a lender seeking the largest income gains from microcredit should concentrate on:
options: neighborhoods that no lender of any kind has previously entered.
borrowers who have had no prior experience with any form of formal credit.
households that were already running a business before they borrowed.
households whose children are not at present enrolled in a school.
communities in which the local moneylenders charge the highest rates.
explanation: The third paragraph reports that later analyses did find gains concentrated in one group, and names it: households that already ran a business before the loan. The randomization was by neighborhood entry rather than by prior lending, and nothing in the passage links larger income gains to inexperience with credit, to school enrollment or to the rates charged by moneylenders.

prompt: Halvorsen Freight measures its safety culture with an annual anonymous survey, and reports improvement because the share of employees describing management as responsive to safety concerns rose from 54 percent to 71 percent over three years. The response rate rose from 38 percent to 84 percent. The safety director concludes that supervisors have in fact become markedly more responsive. The conclusion depends on the assumption that:
options: the employees who began responding once the survey moved into working hours do not differ systematically in their views from those who responded before
the twelve questions retained are the twelve that employees had found easiest to answer honestly
the results of the survey were reported to supervisors in each of the three years covered
no other freight company in the region achieved a comparable improvement over the same period
the number of recorded safety incidents at Halvorsen Freight also fell during the three years

Keston drivers have alternatives to driving downtown comparable to those Bramwell drivers had.

A fee changes behavior by making some other option attractive, so Keston drivers must have options like the ones Bramwell drivers had.
